query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of boron during alloy synthesis will promote interfacial segregation at the FCC/B2 boundaries, thereby pinning these interfaces against premature cracking and inducing a finer recrystallized FCC grain structure during subsequent processing. This should simultaneously increase both strength and ductility in the eutectic HEA.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with coupled FCC and B2 phases in a lamellar/dendritic microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a very small amount (e.g., 0.01–0.02 at%) of boron during melting.
generation.conditions: The boron addition must be homogenized during melting and casting so that it preferentially segregates to the FCC/B2 interfaces. Subsequent conventional thermal treatment (e.g., a standard annealing step) at a temperature sufficient to allow limited recrystallization in the FCC phase without coarsening the B2 skeleton will be applied.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructure with finely recrystallized FCC grains and stabilized, intact B2 interfaces that are reinforced by boron segregation, reducing boundary embrittlement.
generation.mechanism: Boron is known to segregate to interphase and grain boundaries in Ni–Al based intermetallics, reducing the energy of anti-phase boundaries and retarding crack initiation (TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::001). In this eutectic HEA, the boron-enriched interfaces will hinder premature interfacial decohesion during deformation and also act as pinning points that refine the FCC grain size during annealing, enhancing strength via the Hall-Petch effect while preserving ductility by delaying crack propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy (without boron), the alloy with trace boron is expected to show an increased yield and ultimate tensile strength (an estimated improvement on the order of 10–15% if processing is optimized) along with improved uniform elongation (potentially reaching uniform strains in the 30–35% range).
generation.baseline: An as‐cast eutectic HEA without boron addition processed via conventional thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: Excessive boron can lead to the formation of brittle boride phases or excessive grain boundary segregation that may embrittle the material; too little boron might not achieve the desired segregation effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of boron required and its segregation kinetics in a complex HEA, as well as the quantitative improvements on strength and ductility, have inherent uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set with the trace boron addition and one without. Subject both sets to identical homogenization and thermal treatment. Use high-resolution microscopy (EBSD/TEM) to assess grain size and interfacial segregation. Then perform uniaxial tensile testing to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation.
measurements: Grain size distribution and interphase boundary characterization (via EBSD/TEM)
Boron segregation analysis (e.g., atom probe tomography or EDS mapping)
Mechanical properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added alloy does not display a significantly refined FCC grain structure with evidence of boron at the interfaces and if mechanical testing does not reveal simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility beyond the statistical variability of the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In metallurgy and materials science, annealing is a heat treatment that alters the physical and sometimes chemical properties of a material to increase its ductility and reduce its hardness, making it more workable. It involves heating a material above its recrystallization temperature, maintaining a suitable temperature for an appropriate amount of time and then cooling. In annealing, atoms migrate in the crystal lattice and the number of dislocations decreases, leading to a change in ductility and hardness. As the material cools it recrystallizes. For many alloys, including carbon steel, the crystal grain size and phase composition, which ultimately determine the material properties, are dependent on the heating rate and cooling rate. Hot working or cold working after the annealing process alters the metal structure, so further heat treatments may be used to achieve the properties required. With knowledge of the composition and phase diagram, heat treatment can be used to adjust from harder and more brittle to softer and more ductile. The chief issue with polycrystalline Ni3Al-based alloys is its room-temperature and high-temperature brittleness. This brittleness is generally attributed to the inability for dislocations to move in the highly ordered lattices. Researchers focused on addressing this brittleness as it greatly reduced the potential structural applications Ni3Al-based alloys could be used for. However, in 1990 it was shown that the introduction of small amount of boron can drastically increase the ductility by suppressing intergranular fracture. Once this was addressed focus turned to maximizing the structural properties of the alloy. As mentioned, NiAl3-based alloys derive their strength from the formation of γ' precipitates in the γ which strength the alloys through precipitate strengthening. In these NiAl3-based alloys the volume fraction of the γ' precipitates is as high as 80%.

top3.builds_on: The paper shows that tuning the recrystallization behavior of duplex phases can unlock superior mechanical properties. This hypothesis incorporates a compositional modification—inspired by known benefits of boron in Ni–Al systems—to bolster interfacial integrity and refine the microstructure.
top3.what_is_new: It proposes a single alloying intervention (trace boron addition) in the alloy design, rather than a complex thermomechanical cycle, to simultaneously promote strength (via grain refinement) and ductility (via enhanced interfacial cohesion), which was not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of boron during alloy synthesis will promote interfacial segregation at the FCC/B2 boundaries, thereby pinning these interfaces against premature cracking and inducing a finer recrystallized FCC grain structure during subsequent processing. This should simultaneously increase both strength and ductility in the eutectic HEA.
fields.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with coupled FCC and B2 phases in a lamellar/dendritic microstructure.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a very small amount (e.g., 0.01–0.02 at%) of boron during melting.
fields.conditions: The boron addition must be homogenized during melting and casting so that it preferentially segregates to the FCC/B2 interfaces. Subsequent conventional thermal treatment (e.g., a standard annealing step) at a temperature sufficient to allow limited recrystallization in the FCC phase without coarsening the B2 skeleton will be applied.
fields.structural_mediator: A microstructure with finely recrystallized FCC grains and stabilized, intact B2 interfaces that are reinforced by boron segregation, reducing boundary embrittlement.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known to segregate to interphase and grain boundaries in Ni–Al based intermetallics, reducing the energy of anti-phase boundaries and retarding crack initiation (TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::001). In this eutectic HEA, the boron-enriched interfaces will hinder premature interfacial decohesion during deformation and also act as pinning points that refine the FCC grain size during annealing, enhancing strength via the Hall-Petch effect while preserving ductility by delaying crack propagation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy (without boron), the alloy with trace boron is expected to show an increased yield and ultimate tensile strength (an estimated improvement on the order of 10–15% if processing is optimized) along with improved uniform elongation (potentially reaching uniform strains in the 30–35% range).
fields.baseline: An as‐cast eutectic HEA without boron addition processed via conventional thermal treatment.
fields.boundary: Excessive boron can lead to the formation of brittle boride phases or excessive grain boundary segregation that may embrittle the material; too little boron might not achieve the desired segregation effect.
fields.uncertainty: The exact amount of boron required and its segregation kinetics in a complex HEA, as well as the quantitative improvements on strength and ductility, have inherent uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set with the trace boron addition and one without. Subject both sets to identical homogenization and thermal treatment. Use high-resolution microscopy (EBSD/TEM) to assess grain size and interfacial segregation. Then perform uniaxial tensile testing to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation.
measurements: Grain size distribution and interphase boundary characterization (via EBSD/TEM)
Boron segregation analysis (e.g., atom probe tomography or EDS mapping)
Mechanical properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added alloy does not display a significantly refined FCC grain structure with evidence of boron at the interfaces and if mechanical testing does not reveal simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility beyond the statistical variability of the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.builds_on: the general principle, highlighted in both the paper and background literature, that grain boundary segregation and interface modification can enhance ductility and strength by reducing brittleness and promoting beneficial back-stress effects.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a minor compositional tweak via boron doping to refine interfacial structures within the eutectic microstructure, a strategy not explored in the paper, to achieve a synergistic enhancement in mechanical properties.

fields.hypothesis: Introduce a minor boron addition (approximately 0.1–0.2 at%) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA to achieve grain boundary segregation that refines the lamellar interfaces and promotes in situ strengthening without compromising ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with dual-phase (L12 + B2) lamellar microstructure prepared by arc melting and processed by hybrid-rolling.
fields.intervention: Incorporate a small addition of boron (around 0.1–0.2 atomic percent) into the alloy melt prior to casting.
fields.conditions: Maintain high purity and ensure uniform distribution of boron by using rigorous melting protocols (e.g., repeated arc melting and suction casting). The subsequent thermo-mechanical processing (cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling at 600 °C) should be identical to the baseline procedure.
fields.structural_mediator: Boron segregates preferentially to grain boundaries and phase interfaces within the lamellar microstructure, leading to refined interface structures and reducing intergranular embrittlement.
fields.mechanism: Small boron additions are known (e.g., in Ni3Al-based systems) to improve ductility by preventing intergranular fracture through grain boundary strengthening. In the complex eutectic HEA, boron may similarly segregate at the lamellar boundaries, refining the interfaces and promoting better load transfer between the soft and hard phases. This refinement enhances dislocation pinning and increases the back-stress development that postpones the onset of necking, contributing to a simultaneous enhancement of both strength and ductility.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HEA without boron, the boron-modified alloy is expected to show a measurable improvement in both yield strength and uniform elongation. Although the exact magnitude is uncertain, improvements in the range of 5–15% in both metrics are anticipated if interface embrittlement is mitigated.
fields.baseline: Standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA processed by hybrid-rolling without any boron addition.
fields.boundary: Exceeding the small boron content may lead to the formation of coarse and potentially brittle boride phases, which would degrade ductility. The intervention must remain within a low doping regime.
fields.uncertainty: While boron’s beneficial effects are well documented in simpler Ni3Al systems, its behavior in a multicomponent eutectic HEA is less certain, and the optimal boron level needs to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA: one with 0.1–0.2 at% boron addition and one baseline without boron. Process both batches identically via hybrid-rolling and perform tensile tests, as well as microstructural characterization (using TEM, EBSD, and possibly atom probe tomography) to assess grain boundary segregation and interface quality.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and structure (via APT/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added alloy does not exhibit significant simultaneous improvements in yield strength and ductility, or if deleterious boride phases form and negatively impact the microstructure, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.builds_on: The paper demonstrates that strengthening via coherent precipitates (ordered L12) in the fcc phase increases strength without compromising ductility significantly; here, the intervention targets the interfacial regions to further improve work hardening and delay failure initiation.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a compositional intervention (trace boron addition) not reported in the paper and leverages grain boundary chemistry modification to simultaneously enhance strength and ductility.

fields.hypothesis: Trace boron additions can enhance interfacial cohesion in the eutectic HEA by segregating to lamellar boundaries, thereby increasing both strength and ductility simultaneously.
fields.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy (Al0.7CoCrFeNi) with a two-phase lamellar microstructure composed of soft fcc (or fcc + L12 after low‐temperature annealing) and hard B2 + bcc phases.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled amount of boron (e.g. ~0.1–0.3 at.%) via alloying during melting.
fields.conditions: Process under conventional casting, homogenization, and rolling conditions followed by the standard heat-treatment (or even in as-cast condition) used for the alloy; testing at room temperature under quasi‐static and dynamic strain rates.
fields.structural_mediator: Segregation of boron atoms to grain and interlamellar boundaries, leading to enhanced bonding and reduced interfacial embrittlement.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known to segregate to boundaries in related intermetallic systems (e.g. Ni3Al) to suppress brittle intergranular failure. In the eutectic HEA, boron would preferentially decorate the interfaces between fcc and B2/BCC lamellae, thereby lowering stress concentrations at these interfaces. The improved cohesion at the boundaries minimizes premature decohesion while the boron in solid solution may also contribute to solid solution strengthening. This dual action increases the overall yield strength (via boundary strengthening and solution strengthening) and ductility (by reducing crack nucleation at interfaces).
fields.predicted_outcome: Both yield strength and elongation to failure would improve relative to the baseline. While precise quantitative gains are uncertain, improvements on the order of 10–20% in strength and a modest increase in ductility are anticipated.
fields.baseline: The as-processed eutectic HEA (e.g., the CR-H or CR-H-580 conditions as detailed in PMC6478865::web::015 and subsequent sections).
fields.boundary: Effective for eutectic HEAs with lamellar fcc + B2/BCC microstructures similar to Al0.7CoCrFeNi; beyond optimal boron content (>0.5 at.%) risks formation of brittle boride phases.
fields.uncertainty: While analogous improvements have been observed in Ni3Al-based systems (TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::001), the exact magnitude in eutectic HEAs remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloys with incremental boron additions (e.g., 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 at.%) under identical processing routes. Characterize the distribution of boron at the interfaces using TEM/EDS and perform tensile and compression tests at both quasi-static and dynamic strain rates.
measurements: Grain boundary chemistry (via TEM-EDS or atom probe tomography)
Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation-to-failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show statistically significant simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility compared to the boron-free baseline (or if brittle phases form), the hypothesis is falsified.
